newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen up after new record Dow close.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen up after new record Dow close.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open higher Tuesday, following through on a rally which took the Dow industrials to a new record close yesterday.
Analysts said that the industrials, which closed at 7079.39, could easily make a run for the 7100 level today, but whether they close above it is another question..

"The momentum is there. We are only 21 points away. But after the morning followthrough, you are going to have watch the final hours of trading to see what happens," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said stocks would get a boost from a stable bond market and strong markets overseas.

"We will probably open higher. The rally yesterday showed that technical strength in the market remains unabated," he said. "I would think there is a good possibility that we test the 7100 level and a good chance that we close above it."

The Dow could get a lift from Boeing Co, he said. Boeing is negotiating with Delta Air Lines Inc to obtain an exclusive supply agreement, the Wall Street Journal said in its electronic edition Tuesday.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 153.83 points, or 0.85 percent, at 18,267.72.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 16.2 at 4453.6.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, International Business Machines Corp was up 1/8 at 146-1/8 and Sun Microsystems Inc gained 3/8 to 31-5/8.
Elsewhere in the high techs sector, Digital Equipment Corp fell 1/8 to 32 while Hewlett-Packard Co fell 1/4 to 56-1/4.
The dollar eased against the yen and mark in Tokyo and was probing its intraday highs against the mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were flat, with the long bond unchanged to yield 6.82 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that the breakneck expansion of the credit-card business has spelled record profits and soaring stock prices for banks that concentrate on issuing credit cards, known as monoline issuers.

But now intense competition, slowing growth and shrinking profit margins are prompting some of those same companies -- whose appeal to investors until lately has been as pure credit-card plays -- to branch out.

The New York Times Market Place writes that an important part of the securities legislation passed over President Clinton's veto last year gave control over class action lawsuits against companies to the largest shareholder in the group -- not to the lawyers who managed to file the first suit.
